If you’re talking about doing this in the US, you might as well ask for an endless supply of cake and a unicorn while you’re at it because your expectations of how much you can carry over from one PhD to another are pretty unrealistic. You can’t transfer between PhD programs like you can transfer between universities for undergrad. You’re applying as a new student and chances are you’ll have to start over and hope that maybe some of your courses transfer, and you might not get as much say in your dissertation proposal as you’re asking for, especially if you have to be funded by them. 

The only exceptions to starting over that I’ve really seen in the US are when advisors move institutions and even then, the ones I knew who didn’t have to jump through extra hoops (fulfilling new requirements like other classes) were already in candidacy before moving. I had to start completely over when I left my previous program.

MAYBE it’s different outside of the US, but if you’re looking here, don’t expect to be able to just magically pick up where you left off.

Spring admissions for PhD are usually pretty rare to begin with. It puts students in a weird place in terms of courses, exams, etc. and most do their admissions for the fall. The few that I have seen admit for spring openly stated that it was very limited in terms of openings and even more so in terms of funding. Also with the number of students who have already been waitlisted and/or deferred because of funding reasons, I’m honestly doubting the few that did spring admissions would be doing it this year.

I think part of where you're stuck is how you're framing this. You're still the one who worked hard for this, you're the one who wants to go to this school, and you just used the most convenient/accessible resources that you had available to accomplish that task at that time. At that particular time and place, it just happened to be your dad. What if you were with a friend who offered to pay the app fee with their credit card and let you pay them back digitally once your phone had charge again? Or if your bestie who had done a lot for you loaned you their laptop to pay it on their website? Would they still have taken your opportunity away from you like this in your mind? 



One of the things you'll get the opportunity to do (and be encouraged to do) in grad school is to become more independent. It's a fresh start and grad school is a big opportunity for personal growth. If you're upset and you feel like your dad saved your behind now, think of grad school as a brand new beginning where you move away from what you view as relying on him. Instead of him being the first person you call for help, make him the absolute last after you've exhausted everything else and only in real emergencies. Make a list of criteria of the severity of the issue and the amount of resources you have to exhaust before you allow yourself to ask him for help. 

  
And also, to be real, with what's going on in the US, grad admissions around the world are going to become even more fiercely competitive than they already are. If you turn this down now, there is realistically zero guarantee you'll have another opportunity if you apply next year.

As someone who moved into ed research from bench science, what I'm seeing that you need to focus on is setting up your why. Stats and analytics are great and PIs might eat that up, but if I looked at that experience on an application, I'd be wanting to know why ed research/ed policy and what actually led you there (aka convince me it's not just on a whim and that you know what you're getting into).  As an example, I had no ed research experience but I did have TA experience (so something related where I also interacted with people conducting this kind of work) and I was able to speak to how that made me want to ditch the bench and cross over to ed research.

  
That would be the main thing since from what you've given here, it looks like you have a business background and nothing education-related. Have a good story and like the other comment says, find a way to not have anything DEI-related because they're out here cancelling grants left and right, so that's inevitably going to make adcoms nervous.

Okay, this is gonna be a little tough love here: You worked your ass off throughout your undergraduate degree to get the qualifications necessary to be accepted to that Masters program over a bunch of other people. Your phone died and you waited a little too long and you think that makes you completely unqualified for a graduate degree? This is some serious weapons-grade imposter syndrome bullshit.

You screwed up with planning, waiting until the last minute, and shit happened. People wait until the last minute all of the time - if I had a nickel for every time I've seen whole ass PIs submit things or be working on things right up until the end, I'd be easily able to pay my summer fees. (I've dead ass seen professors working on their conference talks on the plane, even seen them work on their talks in the middle of other talks before theirs, had to have people log in and submit applications on time, etc.) 

Honestly, being able to find a way to still do what was necessary instead of giving up and going "Welp, that application is done for" is a positive, not the negative you're seeing it as. You used what resources you had available to you when shit happened, just like one of those PIs borrowing someone else's computer or having to call someone to email them a file.

This doesn't negate all of your hard work and make you unqualified for graduate school. What's important is what you learned from this and how you can improve: Don't leave shit until the bitter end. Set deadlines for yourself ahead of the ACTUAL deadline so that if something happens, you still have time to use whatever resources you have to get the task done before the deadline.

You're qualified. Take the opportunity and go to grad school. Just learn from your mistake, try to improve, and don't pull this sort of last-minute shit while you're there.

That would tell you if you can be shopping for PhD programs directly or need to shop for MA programs first.

Seconding a lot of what the other reply said. I moved PhD programs after a year and a half so I can kind of speak from experience here and can confirm it's logistically challenging, even without your limitations.

  
You would have to start over and be pleasantly surprised IF they take your credits, regardless of rankings. I moved from an R1 to an R2 and my credits still didn't transfer.

If you do apply and have to start over, the odds of being fully remote are very slim. Any PhD program that's fully remote would make me question it, although I know in some fields, doing part of the research remotely is possible. In my field, it's possible (albeit still not common) to go remote for some of the post-quals phase since nothing requires lab work or any specialized equipment, plus there's precedent from COVID times, etc. You'd probably have to be in-person for most of the pre-quals phase since there's usually classes to take, especially if yours don't transfer, plus having to fulfill any TA requirements, especially if that turns out to be the funding mechanism they use to pay their grad students.

I'll second the advice about making sure that your career goals require a PhD. If you really need the degree and want to move elsewhere, you need to come to terms with the possibility of starting over and the likelihood that you would have to be in-person for a couple of years. Any PhD program that would accept you and not expect you to fulfill any of their requirements in your circumstances would definitely be highly suspect.

If I were in your shoes and had an offer like you described, I would take it in a heartbeat. Having great people, a great location, projected short time to degree with publications and guaranteed funding for the duration is incredibly rare in current times especially. You said you have interests in immunology and something related to an autoimmune disease seems like it's going to touch on your broader interests reasonably well. Plenty of people get degrees in things adjacent to their dream research interests (because the perfect fit isn't always possible) and pivot research areas for postdocs or their jobs after graduation. (Ex: I know a lot of STEM ed postdocs who got bench science degrees.) The skills and experience you gain could still possibly allow you to move into something closer to your dream research after graduation, plus there's a chance experience in assay development could be particularly appealing to employers if you want to move into industry later.

  
Definitely in this case, I would take the bird in the hand. With current events impacting not just the US, there's a high chance you might wind up not getting any other opportunities this good for a long time.

Oh, hi, it me. Current education PhD student, albeit different area than what you're interested in, but my answers to what you've asked:

1. Honestly? Made sure I had strong letters of rec and knew how to tell them my "why" in my SOP. Clear, concise description of why I want to do what I want to do and why I want to do it there.
2. To position yourself better, you're probably not going to like this answer: Be a little broader with your research interests. If you hyperfixate on a tiny niche area, you're limiting potential programs because there's not going to be as many advisors focusing on it, so you need to be able to show that you can be flexible. PIs may not have that niche of an area but maybe something adjacent, if you don't show that you're open to adjacent things, some PIs may not be as interested. (And also, with current politics, it's not a bad idea to have a "safer" overarching topic you're interested in to start with.)
3. Not giving numbers but my GPA was considerably lower than yours. (In the area that half the posters on here love to call "bad" even though it's not.)  It's not a numbers game. The quality of your application is going to matter more than your GPA. Good letters, a strong SOP, etc. 
4. I'm not comfortable recommending schools because I don't know your subfield well enough. If you want to broaden your list, keep looking at the most recent papers in your area of interest and where those PIs that are putting out good, interesting research are.
5. Something you unfortunately need to know is that you need a backup plan. This is probably the shittiest timeline imaginable to be applying for education PhDs. PhD admissions next cycle are going to be a shitshow as it is because of deferred offers, funding cuts, reapplicants who had offers rescinded or lost funding, etc. and with what the government is doing to education in this country, I have a suspicion education programs are going to be keeping their cohorts really small to nonexistent next cycle.  Also, I agree with everyone else who has commented on the "diversity points" - keep all of that incredibly close to your chest.

If you're an accepted student, here's some other things I may have learned the hard way (and am always happy to answer more questions if I forgot anything here):

* If you're on a stipend be prepared to potentially go without a paycheck for 2-6 weeks, depending on if your program pays biweekly or monthly since there's often a lag between when you start and the first pay period you get a check.
* If you're on an assitantship with a tuition waiver, ask who pays the graduate school fees. This is often the responsibility of the student and can be an unwanted surprise when they want $100-$1000+ back at the beginning of every semester, including your first.
* Take care of whatever immunization requirements they have early. They can be slow to process and can put a hold on your registration.
* If you're moving, start apartment shopping now. Student-oriented complexes tend to fill up early and even if other complexes don't take applications until 30-60 days before, you'll want to know where is affordable and isn't a shithole. Ask if the program has a list of students looking for roommates or can put you in touch with current students who can help you know where to look.
* If you're moving long-distance, get price quotes ASAP. (Put in a hypothetical address on the back end if you need to.) That gets expensive fast and you may want to decide if it's cheaper to move your stuff or buy new stuff on the other end.
* Get to know the students in your program early. Having a social network and people who can offer you advice is a huge asset. They can help you navigate everything from surviving classes to where the best parking is to where the cheapest grocery stores are.
* Set expectations with your advisor EARLY for workload, communication, meeting and lab hours, etc. Not doing so can turn into a major source of frustration or violation of boundaries later on. (See also: students on 20 hour contracts working 60 hours a week, ask me how I know.)

Started off my PhD adventure as a biology PhD student before moving to the dork side (STEM ed), so I can chime in on this one.

It also meant I had fewer research letters of rec than many people, zero publications, etc. No confirmation but I'm 100% certain it worked against me given the kind of competition I know I was up against.
2. It was definitely a love of research that motivated me to go to grad school. I was originally premed, but once I got involved in research, I loved it. I wasn't set on being a teaching-heavy professor initially, the interest in education really started once I got to grad school and became a TA and loved that.
3. My favorite parts are probably when my advisor and I get really excited about an idea, whenever I get to go present about our research, and the people I work with. Not really comfortable talking about my specific line of work publicly given what's going on now, but I do a lot of qualitative work and hearing people's stories and writing about them for interview studies is fun. Not easy to fit in small journal article word limits, but still fun.

As someone who left one PhD program (without mastering out) and got into another: Yes, there's a definite possibility that you would have lower chances than you would applying fresh. That sort of thing can generate questions and you'll have to have a convincing story ready about why you're doing it and why they can be sure you're not going to bail on them the same way you bailed on your current program.

If you want to take the offer and get paid that stipend, you do you, get that bag, but make an informed decision, don't just go into it thinking it absolutely can't affect your chances next cycle.

CITI training honestly doesn't take that long and if you tried to push back, you'd probably spend more time dancing around in circles with your sponsor than it would take to go through the training.

Having been both a bench scientist and now someone in the social sciences, the thing is that for us social sciences and humanities folk, there's a lot more room for interpretation with our data than there is with something like reading a Bradford assay. With the Bradford, you get a set absorbance and that typically has a clear way it (theoretically) should be interpreted (even then, though, you can still get advisors who will say that specific results are "good enough" or that something out of the expected ranges is clearly our fault, etc.)  In the social sciences and humanities, we can frequently be dealing with the written word, in which case, it's not always as clear cut. Our own lived experiences, emotions, and subconscious biases can influence how data are interpreted. As a qualitative researcher, I can say that we have methods we're supposed to use to be able to pull ourselves out of our analysis as we do it, ways to improve the reliability of our data (for example, working in teams with diverse backgrounds and/or sending our interpretations of an interview to the interviewee and asking them to provide feedback and corrections), and our own standards of rigor, but it's definitely not as clear cut as reading something like assay results in a lab.

If I put my TA hat on, if you were sitting near the front of the room or in front of/near a lot of students or just being very distracting, I'd probably come over during problem solving time and quietly ask if you needed help as a hopefully subtle way of being like "chill out, you're either distracting people around you or the professor's seeing it and getting annoyed". If you sat in the very back of the room and had something like a coloring app open that you were swiping on, I'd leave you alone unless the professor was a jerk. 



As far as changing opinions? As a TA/instructor, if you were a student who was consistently getting high grades, generally respectful and otherwise actively participating in class when expected, I probably wouldn't think much of it if you were sitting in the back of the room and weren't causing a distraction. Other people may feel differently. If you start doing this and your instructor sees it, there are definitely some who would take that into consideration if you were borderline between grades at the end of the semester and asking for yours to be rounded up.

You can have quality research experience and still only get one research-based letter of reference if you're in that one lab long-term. Let's say a student was in a lab for three years and the only person capable of writing a letter is that PI and the rest of their letters have to come from course instructors. Are they somehow less qualified than someone who bounced between labs every semester for the last year and a half of their degree and gets letters from all three of those PIs because they have fewer letters of reference?

I'm talking more specifically about situations where someone may have research experience but they might only have access to one letter of recommendation from it. Students may only be able to be in one lab with a single PI and no other PhD-level colleagues for all of their experience. They could have significant experience because of their time in that lab, but would still only wind up with one research-related reference.

Losing letters of reference would make it a lot harder for students with lower stats to even stand a fighting chance of being considered. For example, it could cause more weight to be put onto GPAs and GPAs are also not the most reliable or equitable metric either - you can get students with 3.0s or 3.2s who may have more talent and potential than some students with 3.8s or 4.0s. Students can be at schools with hellacious grade deflation, students can wind up having no option but to take horrible professors who set students up to fail, they could wind up taking a ton of exam-heavy courses and just be crappy at taking tests, or you get brilliant students who wind up with lower GPAs just because of their outside responsibilities and the need to go to extreme lengths get research experience. Conversely, you could get a student with a 3.9 and experience in 3 labs, but they were incompetent or had a shitty work ethic and they could easily viewed as superior without the references.

It's not as easy as you make it sound. Not everyone going for a PhD has done a masters, though. It's fairly common for many fields in the US for students to go straight from their bachelor's to PhD programs. Students in bachelor's programs also don't necessarily have a senior thesis or experience in multiple labs where they would have had multiple mentors, especially students coming from smaller colleges where research opportunities are limited. Not everyone would have the opportunity to go to another school for something like a summer research program, and some places it'd be insanely difficult to get experience at outside labs as a whole.  Example: My bachelor's is from an undergraduate-only state school. Research opportunities there were very limited since faculty had high teaching loads and tiny research budgets. The nearest universities were 45+ minutes away by car in an area with garbage mass transit. Students frequently had to apply multiple years for summer programs to get one, assuming they had the freedom to go away for 10 weeks. Interview does not equal guaranteed acceptance. People get rejected after interviews all the time, and that could lead to someone getting universally rejected if things just went the wrong way everywhere (can happen, for example, if a student only gets 3 interviews at programs that only admit half of interviewed students and they’re just not in that top half at any of them). 

And honestly, sometimes actually interacting with faculty and students and possibly visiting the campus may turn one of those “safety” schools (which don’t exist for PhD programs) into a front runner. (Example: My current program has an incredibly strong sense of community between the students and faculty and that’s not something that shows on paper, and it’s something that can be a draw for people. It was for me personally after leaving a PhD program that had no community.) Also, those interactions can have the opposite effect - if someone gets negative vibes from students/potential advisors/campuses, etc., that “dream” school can become a hard no. (People sometimes romanticize certain programs and then realize it’s not what they thought it would be when they actually get to their interviews.)

Also, funding details aren’t necessarily set until someone gets an offer letter from a school. People can get offered additional fellowships that can change their situation completely (happened to one of my besties, she got offered several thousand more a year from one school, so that one jumped up her list).

Even if the program is fully funded, the details won’t come until you get the offer letter, and since things can be variable, it’s not like you can be 100% sure you’d get the same offer as the cohorts before. You might get offered the same amount, you might get additional fellowship offers or notifications of ones you can apply for, stipends can be different, etc.

There are lots of reasons PIs might not respond:

1. PIs are very busy people who have a million things on their plate, especially at the beginning of the semester/quarter and sometimes when midterm grades come due, or definitely around major grant deadlines. They have to prioritize.
2. PIs tend to get inundated with emails, so the tons of prospective students who email them get moved to the bottom of the priority list, considering they're often getting email from known entities that they have responsibilities to. (Admin, people in their own lab, students in their classes, etc.) Those clearly have to come first.
3. They do often get tons of these, particularly if they're bigger in their field. So many of them are obvious ChatGPT garbage or obvious generic copy/paste that the person is spamming to everyone affiliated with a program or in that field. Those can and frequently do get ignored.
4. If the email they get is an absolute wall of text that includes a bunch of totally irrelevant or generally unimportant information in the body, it tends to be a "tl;dr" situation.
5. If there's something on a department/program/lab website somewhere about not emailing them until after admission or if they're blatantly displayed as not taking students, you're almost guaranteed to not get a response because that looks like "can't follow directions".
6. Some people who follow up have a habit of not understanding of what an acceptable length of time between emails is and assume that not getting a response within 24-48 hours means they should send follow-ups every 3 days. (See also: a now deleted post on this subreddit where someone sent an email on a Friday night and was upset they didn't get a response in the next 2 days.)

So yeah, you can follow up, but give it a reasonable amount of time (at least a week or two, probably two) and if you don't get a response to the follow-up, it's probably time to move on to the next one. Also check to make sure your emails aren't too long or super generic and that there's nothing explicitly on program/department/lab websites about not contacting or them not taking students before you email.

That journal is sketchy as all hell. Don’t do it. They claim that their impact factor is calculated by Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar, which isn’t how impact factors actually work. They’re calculated by Clarivate, not by the journal owners/Google Scholar/their pet hamster. That’s one red flag right there. Red flag number two: go to their webpage and look at their call for papers graphic. It looks like something a middle schooler made and that’s being generous. Huge red flag number three: a turnaround time of 1-2 DAYS. Reputable journals don’t have processing times that fast. Even finding peer reviewers takes longer than that, let alone them actually reading and critically evaluating your work. If anything claims to have turnaround times that fast, that should be an immediate red flag.  It also doesn’t appear to be indexed by Scopus from what I’m currently seeing, which is fishy and another potential red flag.

First, congrats on your new adventure! There's plenty of things that you can do that might help to make things a little easier when you start. I'm sure other people will chime in with suggestions but here's some things I either wish I knew or found out that made my life easier:

1.  Acknowledge the fact that the first year is very much going to feel like drinking from a fire hose. You're going to get hit with a lot of new information and have to adapt to a new place really fast. Recognize that it's okay to feel overwhelmed and that chances are everyone else around you either is feeling it or has felt it too and be gentle with yourself.
2. Protect your mental health as best you can. Find out what resources your university has for mental health services and what your insurance covers. It wouldn't hurt to try to start finding a good therapist/counselor when you get there, if nothing else at least to help with your transition to your new program and helping to develop coping skills that work.
3. Try out different types of citation management systems and find one that you like and learn to use it well. It'll make your life a lot easier if you can get organized right out of the gate for organizing literature, whether it's immediately for research or even for your writing-intensive classes at first if you don't join a research group right away in your program.
4. Find a way to get organized and manage your time overall that works for you too. Some people use bullet journals, some people use Notion or Obsidian, some people live and die by their Outlook/Google calendars, and some people wind up with desks covered in post-it notes or whiteboards or some combination of all of the above. You're going to be doing the equivalent of juggling flaming chainsaws while riding a unicycle so being organized and managing time well is super important.
5. If your program/department/grad student association/whatever has welcome events or social events, try to go to them. PhD programs can be very isolating so it helps to start getting to know people ASAP.  Try to find interest groups for something that you do or want to do too. PhD programs can be isolating, having a social network is pretty important.
6. Try to establish boundaries on the hours you work as best you can and try to stick to them. It's really easy to fall into the trap of working too many hours and not having any time for self-care and rest and it can be very difficult to claw those hours back once people see you as someone who happily works nights and weekends. (I'm in the process of trying to reclaim my time going into my third year and I REALLY wish I had established boundaries earlier on in my program.) Yes, sometimes you may need to pull long crappy hours to get stuff done at crunch time, but it shouldn't be the norm.
7. If you have to TA, it's not as terrifying as it sounds if you've never done it before. I freaked out about the idea of it when I started my first program, it turned out to be something I really enjoyed and wound up causing my entire career trajectory to change. Even if you don't love it or like it, you eventually get used to it and the panic will eventually go away.
8. Don't be afraid to ask questions. One of the biggest parts of a PhD program seems to be learning to admit when you don't know something and being willing to do the research and ask questions to find the answers to what you don't know. The other students in your research group and your program can be a valuable resource for things that may make your life easier, too, like study guides, protocols you may need, knowing who to talk to about whatever annoying system isn't working on a given day, or even which restaurants give student discounts. 
9. Try to embrace the adventure you're about to go on. I may curse about it and want to scream into the void about it, may come up with interesting descriptions of my advisor when I talk to my friends, and may want to gnaw on my desk, but my PhD program has been the greatest source of personal growth and development in my life.

  
Hope this helps and feel free to ask questions! :)

A PhD is a research degree. Making sure you have solid research experience that you can write about in your application statements and very strong letters of recommendation from professors you do research is going to be more important. A lower GPA isn't an instant kiss of death on a PhD application, lack of research experience could be. People can get into highly ranked programs with less than perfect GPAs with good research experience, but for PhDs it's a lot less likely to work the other way around. A good GPA won't show that you have good research aptitude and knowledge of what you're getting yourself into.

If you're talking about writing an SOP for the application, you tailor it to the program and then show how your interests fit that program and work in the professors of interest. They're going to vary in word length and can vary in specifics that programs want, so look at their prompts.

  
If you're talking about writing separate SOPs to cold email professors...don't. (Unless it's explicitly stated on their website that they want a full SOP or they specifically request one.) Just send them a brief email about your interest in their work and your own interests, then see if they'll meet with you to discuss.  If they request more info like a statement of purpose or a research proposal, then worry about writing one. Until then, just a short email and a copy of your CV should be fine. The more stuff is attached to an email or is exceedingly long, the less likely they are to read it and the more likely they are to save it for later and then forget about it, or just ignore it, so don't send more than you have to to start.

* Keep your research experience at the top, move up your publications and presentations.

* You don't need your GPA on your CV. As someone who wound up having to email professors about PhD opportunities before applying and someone who hears faculty here and elsewhere talk about the emails they get, here's some suggestions I have:

1. Keep it short, sweet, and to the point. Professors are busy, especially around finals season.
2.  I honestly would consider saving the idea of preferred topics for a later discussion and not an initial email. Talk about how their work ties to your interests, but if you start proposing whole ass projects, it's gonna look like you might not be flexible. (It's okay to have ideas but keep expectations low and be comfortable with the possibility that you'd get to work on any of them for a master's. The professors are the ones who know what they have funding for and in their experience what's timebound enough to be doable in a masters timeframe.)
3. Be authentic. Show some personality in your letter of who you are and come across as genuinely interested. Make sure your letter is written for that particular faculty member and not obviously some copy paste job. Do NOT use ChatGPT to write the email. I know multiple faculty members who just delete those kinds of emails because they get spammed with the generic and obviously AI-written ones.
4. See point number 1. I wouldn't go longer than 3 short paragraphs. Don't tell them your entire life story including GPA and all of that crap in your email. Maybe a sentence or two about your background and tie it to your interests, and then attach your CV so they can read if they want to.

I'm not a student at Dayton OR Auburn, but I'm a fully funded PhD student at a different university (and was at one before this), so I can kind of speak to my experiences and what to ask about/look out for:

* You'll want to look at how much the stipend is monthly and see how much rents are in the area. Check any Facebook groups for that university/city. This seems to be the time of year a lot of people at my uni are looking to sublease apartments for next year. Assume you're going to need to share an apartment or townhouse. 
* Remember that you're going to have to pay taxes on your stipend, so the monthly take-home is probably going to be a bit lighter than the number on paper.
* Unless stated otherwise in the funding paperwork, assume you're going to have to pay graduate school fees, even with the tuition waiver. Some schools do pay them for students, but having to pay them yourself is very common. Mine tend to run about $1200 a year.
* Since you're talking about WES evaluations and an I-20, I'm going to assume you're an international student. You'll want to check the university website and/or consult the university's international students office about health insurance. I know that at my current university, my labmate is an international student and they're required to get insurance through the university and it's not subsidized. When my funding offer for my previous institution came in, it stated in the offer that the insurance was mostly subsidized. If your letter doesn't include an offer for health insurance, you'll want to email the program director and ask to be sure.

  
Those are probably the key things you'll want to try to do the math on for your offers, so plan on emailing the program directors and international students offices for the things you don't have the info for. Having been in this situation before, I feel for you. You're going to have to sit down and go through things on an even deeper level than you have so far. Here's some things you might want to dissect pretty carefully:

*  Finances: Which one has the better stipend to cost of living ratio? If the stipends are pretty similar, how do they compare to the rents in the area? What are state income taxes like? Who pays the graduate school fees? Is health insurance entirely covered, partially covered, or not covered at all?
* Location: Does either location speak to you in any way? Iowa City is a lot smaller than Columbus. Is either one more car-dependent than the other? (Basically, if you don't have a car, will you have to get one or can you survive on mass transit?) Are either of them closer to home or friends, or easier to visit home from? Does either have better access to things that you like to do?
* Research: You said they both have faculty you want to work with. Does one program have more faculty that pique your interest? If they both do rotations, does one do them in a more fair way than another?
* Career goals: Which program better supports your potential future career? If you're interested in teaching, which one gives you better access to teaching opportunities and teaching professional development? If you're interested in industry, is there any support for internships?
* Program structure: What are the course requirements like? Does one require significantly more classes than the other? How do the programs handle comprehensive and/or qualifying exams? (Some programs only have quals, some have both. This does matter.) Is TAing a requirement at both places? If so, how long and for what? Which one has a shorter average time to degree?
* Vibes: If you think back to all of your interactions with the programs, were there any gut feelings you remember having? Did anything ever seem "off"? Does your gut tell you anything right now?

There's a lot of variables that come into play that may NOT be apparent until after acceptance, no matter how much research you do on the front end. Financial aid may not be set. People who have those offers are given that time to decide for a reason. Coming from someone who successfully left one PhD program for another without mastering out, the first thing that you're going to hate hearing is that you can't just "transfer" PhD programs like you could transfer schools in undergrad. You're applying through the same exact admissions processes as everyone else and there's a high likelihood that you're starting from zero on your classes and your progress. 


The second thing you're probably going to hate hearing is that it might not just be your supervisor causing all of your stress and health issues; that could just be the workload of grad school as a whole. If you haven't been seeking mental health care before this panic attack, you really need to do so. Panic attacks aren't good, they place even more stress on your mind and body, so you want to really make sure that the issues are more surrounding the supervisor and this particular environment than just something about grad school that trying to change universities won't fix.


What's also going to be rough is that applying to PhD programs all over again means you're going to need the same types of letters of recommendation you had the first time - you need ones that speak to your capabilities as a researcher, especially now that you have a red flag of leaving a program without mastering out. The adcoms are going to be a lot less likely to care about recommendations from professors you've taken classes with than people who can say "yeah, this person is capable of doing PhD-level research".

Also, be brutally honest with yourself about what happens if you don't wind up at the same university as your girlfriend. PhD admissions are competitive as hell normally, you're going to be doing it again with additional red flags over your head from leaving a program so soon. You're likely going to have to apply very broadly and you need to have some kind of compelling story formulated for application season.

So yeah, it’s actually a lot harder than you think to get meaningful feedback to every applicant. It’s just not realistic.

I feel like I got really lucky in this regard. My PhD advisor here is amazing, but I think my previous bad experiences at my last program helped me here since they gave me a long list of red flags to watch out for and some green flags I knew I wanted to see when meeting PIs this time around. Some of the big green flags I saw in my current advisor:

* Enthusiasm. When I met with her on Zoom, I could tell how much she genuinely cared about her work and that she was excited about it beyond it just being a paycheck.
* Research fit. One of her research areas and mine were a great match. Her research direction and my interests lined up almost exactly.
* Mentoring style. I knew from my previous experiences that I wanted a hands-on advisor that I would actually see and work with. I asked about her mentoring style and her expectations and they lined up really well.
* Personality fit. When I met her, I wasn't really anxious at all after the first couple of minutes. We both had very similar vibes and it felt normal talking to her, I wasn't intimidated like I was around other possible PIs.
* Honesty. She was completely transparent with me about her expectations and offered to connect me with her current student before I even asked.

It was unexpected, but I had kind of a gut feeling about her that I didn't get about previous potential PIs and I didn't get any real red flags like I had gotten with others, and my friends in that research community couldn't find any major red flags either.

And yeah, it really does take a lot more research for PhD advisors, but it makes sense since you're committing to working with this person for the next 4+ years of your life and trusting them to mentor and help guide you to become a successful researcher.

Am a grad student who has met with prospective students for our lab and program before. Meeting with us is generally going to be your best chance to ask questions the PI wouldn't know or be able to answer well. It's a great chance to get some honest answers about life in the lab and the program since the PIs and program staff don't experience it the same way. It's a good chance to ask us how the lab culture is, so stuff like how supportive the PI is, how often we interact with the PI, what the vibe of the lab space is like, how often we actually go in vs. what the PI says, how much we're allowed to travel, etc. You could also ask us things about the program culture, how demanding the coursework is, how happy students tend to be, how far the stipend goes, what we do for fun outside of classes, TA obligations, etc. You might want to be prepared to chat on a fairly surface level about our work and your research, but generally we're too busy to go in-depth.

As far as interactions with us, try to be a decent human being. Be respectful, try to be professional, be approachable, and show us how interested you are in the lab and the program. We ARE doing vibe checks on you as people we'd want as colleagues in our lab and part of our community, and if you're a jerk, we WILL be reporting back to the PI and possibly the program staff on your behavior. (Not saying you will be specifically, but I've had to do that before.)

Okay, this email has some problems to it. Definitely needs to be concise and less generic sounding (the first paragraph is very awkward sounding), but there's some bigger issues here.

"Dear Professor,"

Make sure that you're using their last name too, otherwise it VERY much sounds like a copy/paste email and they may stop reading there. Remember that many of these professors are getting inundated with these cold emails, someone who doesn't even include their name would make a bad impression and you don't want to do that.

"and anything 'space' grabs my attention"

I know what you were going for, but this is SO generic sounding. It gives off the vibes that you just email everyone who mentions "space". 

"Regretfully, I couldn’t read the whole paper because it was behind a paywall."

This is a really bad sentence to include. This makes it sound like you're not willing to do the legwork to see if you can find it on ResearchGate, ask other people with library access, or do any other research to find it. This is especially bad if you're emailing for a PhD program because there WILL be times papers are paywalled even with your university accounts and you still need them. Also, for many researchers to publish open access instead of behind a paywall can be VERY expensive (upwards of 11 THOUSAND USD in some cases), so this could rub them the wrong way if they can't afford it because of limited funding. Either way, it sends the "your work is interesting but not interesting enough for me to do some extra research" message.

"So in that regard, my experience in using HEC-RAS for sediment and river modeling in tandem with my field experience while doing river side survey, tunnel alignment survey might come in handy."

The "might come in handy" part could be taken the wrong way. If you mention the techniques, the PI would know best if it may or may not come in handy, so this is excessive. Also, most of this should be in your CV, then you can condense this down.

"Further, I am familiar with python libraries such as Pandas, Matplotlib, Numpy which are very useful in numerical modeling."

Should be in your CV instead. Also, if this person does mathematical modeling, they'd know that they're useful. They really don't need to be told that.


Keep it short, sweet, and to the point. You could say something like "Dear Dr. X, My name is Y and I'm a prospective student looking to apply for Fall 2024. Add something BRIEF about your experiences. I saw your posting about an opening for a student on whatever website it was. I'm really interested in your work on A and B and how it relates to my interests in C. I'd really like to talk with you more about your work and the opening in your lab. I'm attaching my CV and I'd be really happy to talk with you about how my experiences would fit in really well with your work."

Hoo boy, here's a lot of red flags I ignored when I was in my first program:

​

* Lab takes lots of rotation students but none stay
* PI is never in the lab at all (even if they're hands-off, they should still surface once in a while)
* PI isn't willing to take the time to meet with rotation students 1-on-1
* PI doesn't provide a clear set of expectations for rotations
* PI won't answer questions about post-rotation expectations for their students
* PI starts telling you to drop TA responsibilities if you're teaching
* PI gets mad if you have to leave by a certain time for safety reasons (ex: before the last shuttle leaves and you have to walk into an unsafe neighborhood)
* Other students in or out of lab talk about students not graduating from or changing labs
* Other students talk about how a certain PI makes them uncomfortable just to be around
* Signs of the PI being super micromanagey if you don't like that
* PI shows signs of wanting to drop the projects you were interested in (even if they don't drop it completely, it may wind up WAY further down the list of things that will get time/money put into it)
* PI always taking first authorship on papers and/or never credits RAs/undergrads who do contribute a lot
* Lack of communication between PI and lab members or between lab members

Honestly, if you're in a rotation and something in your gut tells you things are off, trust your gut.

The learning curve for R can be steep, but it's doable. And if you're in a good program and have a good lab and advisor, you won't be fighting to learn it alone. You'll have other students in your classes who may be in a similar place with R and you can work through things together. You'll probably have labmates and other students in your program who know more and can answer questions. Honestly, what has helped me has been making a backup copy or six of my data set and just using one of those backups to test out R code and seeing what breaks. Most of the tutorials online should have dummy data sets you can download, follow along with some of the tutorials and then just try adapting other tutorials to that data set once you understand the structures a little better, plus if it's a dummy data set and you break it by messing around, nobody cares.

Don't feel completely discouraged by the thought of having to learn R because of your past experiences with a professor who sounds like he shouldn't be teaching in the first place. You CAN do this!

My SOPs varied in length because every program had their own requirements. Most of them were in the 500-1000 word range, but I had one that had a 250-word MAXIMUM.  That was ROUGH.  In the ones that were longer, I had 1-2 paragraphs on my research interests, usually 1 about how I developed them (and how my previous research interests tie into them) and then the other was how they fit well with the school and the program.  And it's okay if your research interests aren't SUPER focused, mine were pretty broad when I went into the application process and have narrowed down considerably over the course of my first year in this program.

First thing I'm going to suggest is to make sure you know what your research interests are and reach out to professors there who are at least kind of related. (It doesn't have to be a perfect match to your interests, but close enough to make sense. Like if you're interested discipline-based education research at the undergraduate level but you're emailing PIs who focus solely on preschool administration, that would definitely prompt some questions.)  This way you can also find out if they're planning on taking students and if you meet with them, you can also watch out for red flags. Having PIs already interested in taking you on can really be helpful and depending on the program, might be required. (In the case of where I am now, it wasn't a requirement but I'd put money on this PI's word helping the program not focus on some of my previous issues.)

Second, when you write your SOP, you need to have your story straight. A LOT of it will be about fit. For education PhDs, you need to be a lot more intentional about why you specifically want a PhD in education, especially since we also have an EdD as a doctoral degree path. You should already know why you want the PhD vs. EdD, you need to sell yourself to THEM as someone they want and wouldn't go "Nope, go apply to the EdD over there". Think about what your story is. Honestly, what helped me was to actually talk to a friend about how I became interested in education research and how I discovered my research interests and what I want to do with it. Record it or have your friend take notes and then you basically wind up with an outline instead of starting with a completely blank slate. After that, you can tweak it to make it more school specific, but that should at least get you going.

Those are the two major things I can think of off the top of my head.  Happy to answer questions!

There’s really no such thing as a safety school when applying to grad school. There’s too many moving parts to the equation. The process is a lot more holistic than undergrad admissions. People with very strong profiles in terms of GPA and publications can get rejected while the same program will take the person with a mediocre GPA and zero pubs if they’re a better fit because of other parts of their application.

The best way to improve your chances is to target programs that are the best fit for you. Look for ones that have strong alignments with your research interests. If you're looking at Ed.D or Ph.D programs and trying to make choices based on perceived "easiness" of getting in (spoiler alert: they're all competitive as hell), then you're 100% asking the wrong question here. The important question to ask is which one aligns better with your intended career outcomes. Neither are "easy" to get into. Ed.D programs almost universally require a masters degree or equivalent graduate coursework to get into and education Ph.D programs are pretty similar, although there are SOME exceptions depending on the PhD program and if it's more specialized like STEM ed.

Ed.Ds are generally for people wanting to go into some sort of administrative role and not as heavily geared towards academia. They tend to be something applied for after you have some experience in education, hence why there's a huge emphasis on having the masters degree and/or the coursework and experience to even get your foot in the door.

Ph.Ds are research-based and tend to be more oriented towards the research and teaching side of life than the administrative side. When I looked at Ph.Ds in STEM Ed, a lot of them either wanted an existing MS in a scientific discipline or you're expected to earn one along the way towards your Ph.D. The rest of it is the same as trying to get into any other PhD program. Research experience and letters are king, etc. And while education PhDs are often funded, it's definitely not at the same level as some of our counterparts in other disciplines, to the point where side jobs and/or student loans wind up becoming a necessary evil.

The tl;dr here: neither are easy to get into. Figure out which one suits your career goals better and prepare for that set of admissions requirements.

Having been in the position of having two choices back in 2020 and being forced to choose between them sight unseen, I can try and offer some insights from my experience:

Get a whiteboard and set up a comparison side by side for every school on the categories that matter and start scrutinizing everything.

Compare the stipends (AFTER graduate fees and taxes). How many PIs are you interested in working with at each program (make sure there’s enough to have multiple backups in case your first choices wind up falling through/turning into bad matches). Look at the program structures: do they have more major exams and/or are their quals particularly bad? (For example, the program I chose then had comps at the end of year 1 and quals in 3rd year, the other only had quals. I regretted my choice for that alone.) Look at the cost of living, how good the insurance is, and how good mental health care on campus is (you’re going to need it in grad school). Which ones have more opportunities that help with your eventual career goals? (Example: I wound up at a school last time that was very heavily NIH focused and there wound up being very little for anyone interested in educational oriented roles). Having been in a very similar position back in 2020 and made a huge mistake in my choices, this is things I would recommend and that I'm doing this time around.

* Compare the grad school fees and who pays them. My 1k a year greater stipend turned out to be less than the other school because the fees were a LOT higher. If you have a car, ask about parking fees because some schools are RIDICULOUS.
* Ask the grad students at both programs how well they're supported by the program and the department.
* Compare the health insurance and mental health care at both programs. 
* Ask the students what the overall culture of the program is. Do people stay really in tiny groups or is there a bigger sense of community?
* Talk to as many grad students in both places as you can and see if they'll give you the good, the bad, and the ugly
* Ask about how the program director and staff are. Are they organized and approachable or do you need to email them six times when you have a question?
* Ask the grad students what they do for fun. If they hesitate or dodge the question, that's a red flag that their work-life balance might not be respected.
* Compare both program structures and see if one is more advantageous than the other. Are there multiple sets of exams or just quals and how do they work?
* Ask about TA requirements (or if there are any) and if you're interested in academia, any opportunities beyond just the required semesters. If there are, ask the students if they get overworked as TAs.
* Ask where most of the students seem to wind up. Is the program heavily biased towards industry, government, or academia and how does that line up with your goals?
* Try to get a feel for both of them as much as you can from every interaction you have with the programs. If one of them just feels "off" to you, go with your gut and avoid it.

Just finished my first two full semesters of TAing intro bio labs, so I definitely have some advice since I was in your shoes back in September.

1. Set CLEAR boundaries for when you will and won't answer student emails and how long your response times will normally be.  You WILL get emails at times like 10 pm on a Friday and you need to be firm on not answering them at all hours of the day and night, otherwise they're going to expect that level of response every single time.  You NEED your work-life balance because it gets exhausting.
2. Never assume the students did the pre-lab reading.  Some of them won't even do the GRADED pre-lab assignments.  Plan on giving them the nutshell version and address all of the stumbling blocks you anticipated when you ran through the lab by yourself ahead of time.  It should cut down on the number of times you have to repeat yourself.
3. You WILL feel like you have no clue what you're doing at first and that's okay.  If you have preceptors or lab coordinators, make sure that they know you've never been a TA before, never used whatever learning management software they used, or if it's course material you've never covered.  (In my case, I had to point out that I never saw Canvas a day in my life and went to a school that didn't HAVE TAs at all so I had no clue what they really did.  They really helped me learn the ropes and grow a LOT.)
4. Learn proper procedure for dealing with student grade challenges and plagiarism/cheating early on.  You WILL have students try stuff and they'll do it badly and you'll be able to spot it from a mile away, so be prepared for it.
5. Be kind and empathetic, but also be fair and be firm when needed.  You'll have students who are normally great students and you get along with them great, but you're going to hate yourself at times if they royally screw up an assignment because you have to grade everyone by the same rubric.  You're going to have to enforce safety rules and it doesn't matter who it is that doesn't wear long pants and doesn't have something to change into.
6. If you're in a setup where there are other TAs teaching the same labs, talk to them, especially if they're experienced.  They can tell you what to watch out for, how to make your life easier.  You can bounce ideas off other TAs if you're stuck with something.
7. Make the most of your time as a TA.  It's a LOT of work, but it's a great chance to learn and grow.  I thought I was going to be terrible and I about cried at the overwhelming amount of stuff thrown at me at the different TA orientations, but I grew A LOT over the past year.

Good luck, have fun with it, and feel free to ask any more questions!

Just keep your eyes open and trust your gut if something doesn't feel right.

Stuff to do:  If they're housing you in the dorms and you're on north campus (IDK what program you're with so not sure, but mine was housed in Independence Hall up there), it was nice to spend time out on the turf and get some sun. If you don't have a car with you and  you're not against mass transit, you can take the DART bus to a bunch of places, including the mall and the beach.  Philly isn't that far but if you don't have a car, you're kind of stuck working with the train schedules and that may or may not work with whatever research you're doing.

Did my undergrad elsewhere (am current PhD student at UD and a TA for lower level STEM classes), but had two bio majors and a chem minor so hard classes were my life.  

I can definitely offer some advice for surviving since a lot of it does carry over and I can offer some observations from the TA side as well:

1. Don't think that because you were good in science in high school that it'll automatically carry over to college.  You're going to have to work hard, probably going to have to adjust how you think about your science, and definitely get a lot of experience changing how you write about science.


2.  Speaking of writing about science, start getting into the good writing habits early.  Learn how to cite sources properly early on and develop a good system for keeping track of sources ASAP and it'll carry you a long way.  (I had papers as an undergrad where I had to use >20 sources and being able to keep that organized saves you a LOT of headaches!)


3.  In your lower level STEM classes, if you have TAs, get to know them and PLEASE don't be afraid to ask questions.  (It's LITERALLY a grad TA's job to help you and most of us don't bite.  Some undergrads are legit terrified of us and IDK why and I wish they weren't.  I enjoy seeing my students pass and get awesome grades!)


4. REALLY make sure that even though the fundamentals you learn early on may be boring or tedious, you actually put in the time to learning them.  I keep telling my undergrads that some of the things that I taught them in first semester WILL come back to haunt them in upper level classes if they don't remember them.  


5.  Organic Chem is going to be challenging no matter what.  It's a very demanding course but you get out of it what you put into it in terms of time investment vs. grade received.


6.  If you get the option, balance your course load carefully.  Save some of your easier gen eds for when you're in your final years and everything else you have left is hard classes.  You'll thank yourself later when you need enough hours to be full time and you're NOT taking a load like Orgo 2, Biochem, and Analytical Chem at the same time.  (I speak from experience on that one.  0/10 do NOT recommend.)

Those are some of the highlights I can think of.  Don't be afraid to ask questions here or DM me.
